Title: Who has jurisdiction over the flydubai incident?
Article:
LETTER:
A reported cockpit assault aboard flydubai flight FZ1073 on Sept 30, 2026, may have begun as a violent confrontation at over 9,000 metres. Legally, however, its consequences stretch across three countries.
The aircraft left Dubai, was registered in the United Arab Emirates (UAE), and was flying through Saudi Arabian airspace when the alleged confrontation took place before making an emergency landing in Tabuk.
The Indian captain reportedly suffered serious injuries. The co-pilot was detained for investigation. The aircraft also reportedly entered a rapid descent before passengers and crew intervened.
The immediate questions are straightforward: What happened? Who was responsible? What caused the descent?
The harder question is: who has the legal authority to investigate and prosecute?
This is where international aviation law becomes particularly important. Saudi Arabia, the UAE and India each have a legitimate connection to the incident, but those connections arise from different legal principles.
Saudi Arabia has the most obvious territorial connection.
The alleged offence reportedly occurred while the aircraft was in Saudi airspace. Under Article 1 of the 1944 Chicago Convention, every state has complete and exclusive sovereignty over its airspace.
That gives Saudi Arabia a substantial basis for investigating what happened. The fact that the aircraft landed in Tabuk strengthens that position.
The suspect, witnesses and potentially important evidence are also within Saudi jurisdiction. But the UAE cannot simply be written out of the picture.
The aircraft was UAE-registered. Under the 1963 Tokyo Convention, the state of registration has jurisdiction over offences committed aboard its aircraft.
The 1971 Montreal Convention also requires states to establish jurisdiction over specified offences committed aboard aircraft registered in their territory.
In other words, the same incident can legitimately engage Saudi territorial jurisdiction and UAE aircraft-registration jurisdiction. That does not mean the two countries must compete for control.
The Lockerbie case offers a useful warning against simplistic conclusions.
Following the 1988 bombing of Pan Am Flight 103 over Scotland, Libya brought proceedings before the International Court of Justice against Britain and the United States.
In 1998, the ICJ confirmed jurisdiction under the Montreal Convention. But it did not determine an exclusive criminal jurisdiction for the bombing.
The lesson is important. International aviation law often operates through overlapping jurisdictional interests rather than a single rule declaring one state automatically supreme.
India adds another dimension. The injured captain is reportedly Indian.
International law recognises the passive personality principle, under which a state may, subject to its domestic law and international obligations, exercise jurisdiction over certain offences committed against its nationals abroad.
Yet, nationality alone does not automatically make India the lead investigating state. India's most immediate role is likely to involve consular assistance, protection of its national and cooperation in securing relevant evidence.
There is also an important distinction between criminal investigation and aviation safety investigation.
Under ICAO Annex 13, the state of occurrence generally conducts the technical investigation.
Saudi Arabia would therefore have a central role if the incident occurred within its territory or airspace, while the UAE, as the state of registration and operator, would have recognised participation rights.
This distinction matters. Determining why an aircraft descended is not necessarily the same legal exercise as determining whether a criminal offence occurred.
What should happen next? The answer should not be a jurisdictional contest.
Saudi Arabia should lead the territorial criminal investigation, while the UAE should exercise its rights as the aircraft's state of registration. India should provide consular and evidentiary assistance concerning the injured captain.
The three countries should coordinate access to cockpit evidence, flight recorders, medical records, crew statements and operational data.
Evidence must be preserved, procedures respected and any prosecution conducted according to the jurisdiction ultimately exercised under applicable law.
The flydubai incident is a reminder that modern aviation routinely crosses legal borders.
An aircraft can be registered in one country, operated from another, fly through the airspace of a third and carry nationals from many more. International aviation law therefore cannot depend on a simple winner-takes-all approach.
Its real test is whether states can exercise their legitimate jurisdiction while cooperating sufficiently to establish the truth and ensure accountability.
At over 9,000 metres, national borders may seem invisible. In law, they remain very real. The challenge is ensuring that those borders do not become barriers to justice.
R. PANEIR SELVAM
Principal Consultant
Arunachala Research & Consultancy Sdn Bhd (ARRESCON)

Title: Show decorum, respect Dr M's family privacy, Fahmi tells content creators
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Content creators, influencers and social media users should prioritise decorum, consideration and humanity when generating content, particularly regarding the latest situation involving Tun Dr Mahathir Mohamad.
Communications Minister Datuk Seri Fahmi Fadzil said that while many were eager to know about the former prime minister's health status, not everything needed to be turned into news or social media content.
"Technology may evolve and we may hold differing views, but let us not use social media to the extent of losing our decorum, morals and humanity," he said in a video uploaded on X last night.
Fahmi urged all parties to give Dr Mahathir and his family space and time to grieve following the passing of Tun Dr Siti Hasmah Mohd Ali.
He said Dr Mahathir's son, Datuk Seri Mukhriz Mahathir, had earlier requested that the family's privacy be respected during their period of mourning.
Meanwhile, Fahmi reminded social media users not to spread speculative posts, insensitive artificial intelligence (AI)-generated material or inappropriate comments.
"If we come across humiliating content, insensitive AI material or posts wishing ill upon others, do not share, comment or give them views.
"If you see such content, report it directly to the Malaysian Communications and Multimedia Commission (MCMC) or the police," he added.

Title: JB-Singapore RTS Link passenger service delayed to February
Article:
JOHOR BARU: The Johor Baru-Singapore Rapid Transit System (RTS) Link passenger service has been delayed to February, with final systems tests and trial runs expected to be completed by the end of this year.
Singapore's RTS Operations Pte Ltd (RTSO), the train service operator, said the revised timeline remained subject to independent safety certification and final regulatory approvals from Malaysia and Singapore.
In a statement yesterday, RTSO said it expected to complete all systems tests and trial runs by Dec 31, followed by safety certification by an independent safety assessor.
"Taking into account the expected duration of works and the estimated duration required for safety certification from a third party and approval by both Grantors, passenger service is expected to begin in February 2027.
"Singapore Land Transport Authority and the Transport Ministry have been informed of the revised timeline," the statement read.
RTSO said infrastructure works in both countries were complete and remained on track to support passenger service once the remaining testing and commissioning activities were completed.
The New Straits Times contacted Transport Minister Anthony Loke, who confirmed that the RTS Link operation had been delayed to February.
However, Johor Works, Transportation, Infrastructure and Communications Committee chairman Mohamad Fazli Mohamad Salleh said he had learnt of the delay through media reports from Singapore.
The much-anticipated cross-border rail service is designed to ease congestion at the Causeway and improve daily connectivity between Johor Baru and Singapore.
The RTS Link will connect Bukit Chagar in Johor Baru with Woodlands North in Singapore, with a peak capacity of up to 10,000 passengers per hour in each direction.
The journey between the two stations is expected to take about five minutes.
Co-located Customs, Immigration and Quarantine (CIQ) facilities at both stations will allow commuters to complete immigration clearance at their point of departure.
RTSO is a joint venture between subsidiaries of Prasarana Malaysia Bhd and SMRT Corporation Ltd.

Title: 77-year-old man missing after car plunges into river
Article:
SUNGAI PETANI: A 77-year-old man is missing after the car he was driving skidded into a river along Jalan Lubuk Segintah-Lubuk Kawah here early this morning.
A search and rescue (SAR) operation has been launched for Mat Yusof Hashim of Jalan Masjid Felda Teloi Timur.
Kuala Muda district police chief Assistant Commissioner Hanyan Ramlan said police received a call from a member of the public about 1am today informing them of an accident involving a car that had skidded into a river.
He said preliminary investigations showed that Mat Yusof was driving from Jalan Kuala Ketil towards Teloi Timur Felda.
"The victim is believed to have lost control of the car before it skidded into the river. Initially, the victim was believed to have drowned along with the vehicle.
"However, after the submerged car was lifted from the river using a crane, an inspection found that the driver was not inside the vehicle," he said in a statement today.
Hanyan said firefighters continued the SAR operation in the area around the river, while the car was sent to the Kuala Muda Traffic police station.
"The status of the victim remains unknown at this time," he said.
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Bahrain F1 Grand Prix: Fans frustrated by hours-long waits for shuttle buses
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Formula 1 (F1) fans have expressed frustration over the management of free shuttle bus services at the Sepang International Circuit (SIC), with some claiming they had to wait for hours to board buses after leaving the venue yesterday.
One of them, who attended the first day of the F1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix 2026 yesterday, claimed he had waited four hours before managing to board a shuttle bus.
In a Threads post, a user identified as @dan_anyeal claimed he had queued for public transport about 5pm but only managed to board a bus four hours later.
"I started queuing about 5pm, but only managed to board a bus about 9pm. Four hours.
"I am really disappointed with the transport management today. If there are no improvements, things could get even worse on Saturday and Sunday," he said in his social media post last night.
Several photos shared in the post showed scores of F1 visitors stranded by the roadside while waiting for shuttle buses to take them home, with the situation becoming tense amid claims of an altercation.
It was previously reported that Rapid KL would provide 95 buses for a dedicated shuttle service operating between designated locations and SIC during the event, which runs from yesterday until tomorrow.
The dedicated shuttle service to SIC is provided from the Level 1 Bus Hub at Kuala Lumpur International Airport (KLIA) Terminal 2, the Mitsui KLIA Bus Hub and De-Village, Persiaran Millenia 2, Bandar Baru Enstek, Negri Sembilan.
Meanwhile, the user also urged the management to take action before the situation worsened.
[[nid:1546579]]
"We came here for F1, not to spend almost half the evening waiting for buses.
"Is this how you manage transport for more than 100,000 F1 fans who have been waiting so long for this moment?" he said.
Another Threads user, @ryanmahowlett, claimed he left the Sepang area about 5.45pm but only managed to board a bus about 9pm.
"Leaving Sepang today was one of the craziest things I've ever experienced.
"People were fighting, throwing things at the buses, shouting and screaming," the user said.
He added that it was among the worst-managed situations he had ever seen.
"Without a doubt, one of the most badly organised things I've ever seen.
"When we exited Sepang, there were absolutely no signs or information. It was outrageous.
"I hope everyone was safe and able to get home safely in the end," he said.

Title: #NSTViral: 'Even robots get nervous': Shaky android amuses Netizens [WATCH]
Article:

The short clip, posted on Threads by user rinaa_khairull, showed the android holding items during the 2026 National Digital Library Seminar on Tuesday while repeatedly trembling and shifting on the spot.
She captioned the video: "Point of view: Me after cutting sugar for half a day."
The clip has garnered more than 60,000 views and 1,700 likes.
View on Threads

Another user, n__aliahatiqah, wrote: "POV: after breastfeeding."
The robot's shaky appearance quickly became the unexpected highlight of the otherwise formal event, with social media users joking that it appeared to be battling a serious case of stage fright.

Title: Four areas in Sarawak and Johor record unhealthy API as haze persists
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Four air quality monitoring stations recorded unhealthy Air Pollutant Index (API) readings as of 8.30am today, with Sri Aman, Sarawak recording the highest reading at 151.
According to the Department of Environment's Air Pollutant Index Management System (APIMS), Serian was the other air quality monitoring station in Sarawak to record an unhealthy API reading, at 120.
The other two stations recording unhealthy API readings were in Pasir Gudang and Larkin, both in Johor, at 147 and 110 respectively.
Sixty-one air quality monitoring stations recorded moderate API readings, while two stations recorded good API readings.
No stations recorded API readings at very unhealthy or hazardous levels as of 8.30am today.
An API reading of zero to 50 indicates good air quality, 51 to 100 moderate, 101 to 200 unhealthy, 201 to 300 very unhealthy, while readings above 300 are hazardous.
Meanwhile, the Malaysian Meteorological Department (MetMalaysia), in a statement issued at 7am, said thunderstorms, heavy rain and strong winds were expected in several states this morning.
The warning covers Sepang, Kuala Langat and Klang in Selangor; Port Dickson in Negri Sembilan; Melaka; and Tangkak and Muar in Johor.
In Sarawak, a similar warning was issued for Betong, including Kabong, Pusa and Saratok; Sarikei; Mukah; Bintulu; Limbang; Kapit, including Kapit, Bukit Mabong and Belaga; and Sri Aman, including Sri Aman and Lubok Antu.
In Sabah, the warning covers the Interior, namely Beaufort, Kuala Penyu and Sipitang.
According to MetMalaysia, a thunderstorm warning is issued when there are signs of rainfall with an intensity exceeding 20mm per hour that is imminent or expected to continue for more than an hour.
"Thunderstorm warnings are short-term warnings valid for no more than six hours for each issuance," it said.

Title: Oil tankers attacked in Hormuz strait: UK maritime agency
Article:
TEHERAN: Two oil tankers have been struck by "unidentified projectiles" in the Strait of Hormuz region, a British maritime agency said Friday, in the latest threat to shipping in the waterway.
The Hormuz passage, through which a fifth of the world's oil and LNG passed before the US and Israel launched strikes against Iran in late February and sparked the Middle East war, remains at the heart of the conflict.
Teheran has been blocking the passage of commercial ships, firing on vessels it accuses of unauthorised crossings.
Washington responded with a counterblockade of Iranian ports in an effort to prevent Teheran from exporting its oil.
The first attack caused "a small fire and blackout onboard", the UK Maritime Trade Operations agency said Friday, adding that the fire was later extinguished.
There were no reported casualties or environmental impact, it added.
The vessel, which was exiting the strait, was able to resume its journey, UKMTO said, without specifying the ship's ports of origin and destination.
Hours later, another crude oil tanker reported being struck by an "unknown projectile" east of Oman, with all crew safe and no environmental damage reported, according to the UKMTO.
The agency said authorities were investigating the incidents. — AFP

Title: Bahrain F1 Grand Prix: Visitors stuck for hours as congestion hits SIC, KLIA2
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Visitors leaving the Sepang International Circuit (SIC) after the first day of the Formula 1 Gulf Air Bahrain Grand Prix 2026 yesterday had to endure unusual traffic congestion.
The congestion extended to Kuala Lumpur International Airport Terminal 2 (KLIA2), where visitors were forced to queue for the Express Rail Link (ERL) to continue their journey home.
Videos shared on social media showed queues of passengers filling the second floor of KLIA2, believed to include visitors making their way home after leaving SIC.
A Threads user, @ishvinderjitsingh, claimed he left SIC about 7pm but only arrived at KLIA2 about 9.30pm.
"I left SIC about 7pm, reached KLIA Terminal 2 about 9.30pm and now I have to wait for the ERL.
"After more than three hours, I am still around KLIA and Sepang. Please make things easier," he said.
Another user questioned the frequency of the ERL service, claiming trains were operating only every 20 minutes despite the high number of passengers.
A similar situation was shared by Threads user @userww4687, who claimed the journey home became more difficult as congestion occurred not only at SIC but also continued at KLIA2.
"From day until night, that is the problem. When it was finally time to go home, even taking a Grab cost RM150 from KLIA2 because the ERL was also congested.
"Crowd management should have been planned earlier, with dedicated lanes provided either for the public or shuttle buses," the user said.
Earlier, social media was flooded with posts from visitors about unusual congestion when leaving SIC, with some claiming they had to wait for hours to board shuttle buses to parking areas and nearby transport hubs.
The situation also prompted calls for improved traffic flow management, greater shuttle bus capacity and better coordination of public transport to cope with the large number of visitors throughout the event.
In the comments section, the user also claimed that e-hailing fares had reached more than RM90 at the time, prompting the user to continue waiting for public transport.

Title: 'PJ MP's resignation another blow to PKR, but PH remains largely intact'
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Lee Chean Chung's resignation is another blow to PKR, with the party now struggling to retain even its own lawmakers.
International Islamic University Malaysia political scientist Dr Syaza Shukri said with Lee being the fourth PKR member of parliament to leave, the party had lost more than 10 per cent of the 31 it started out with following the 15th General Election.
This, she said, showed that PKR was in "emergency mode".
"This is really bad for PKR. It is almost a bloodbath, considering that is four out of 31, more than 10 per cent.
"On one hand it's not a surprise or coming out of nowhere but it shows that PKR is really in emergency mode.
"They are not winning over new voters (based on recent elections) and can't even keep their own MPs," she told the New Straits Times.
She said while PKR could argue that it still had other credible leaders, the recent trend did not suggest voters were gravitating towards the party.
On the impact of Lee's resignation on Pakatan Harapan, Syaza said the coalition remained intact but its internal dynamics could change as its component parties faced different challenges.
"The most stable party is Amanah, but it is not that strong or influential. DAP and PKR have issues, but DAP remains the biggest party.
"PKR, as people always say, cannot get away from the accusation that it is 'Anwar's party', and all these resignations are not helping to create a formidable party beyond Anwar," she said.
[[nid:1546593]]
Drawing a comparison with Umno's experience after GE15, Syaza said political parties could regain support after periods of decline if they were able to rebuild confidence.
"It is all about confidence. Umno was at the bottom back in 2018, so people left, but slowly Umno regained its confidence from continuing to be in government.
"PKR is now at the bottom because of criticism over its administration, since the prime minister is from PKR, so people are leaving.
"If you ask me, it is a normal swing in politics. Maybe PKR, and by extension DAP, can regain confidence once they are back in opposition again," she said.
However, Syaza said PKR's position could still change depending on how the government performs, particularly with the upcoming 2027 Budget and institutional reforms.
"But right now, yes, PKR has reached its peak, unless it can turn things around with the upcoming Budget and institutional reforms," she said.
Meanwhile, Universiti Teknologi Malaysia Faculty of Social Sciences and Humanities director Associate Professor Dr Mazlan Ali said Lee's resignation as an MP and from PKR was expected and would have limited immediate impact on the government.
"The resignation of the Petaling Jaya MP comes as no surprise; in fact, it was expected.
"PMX (Datuk Seri Anwar Ibrahim) and his government remain unaffected by this. PKR is already prepared for this possibility," he said.
Mazlan said as long as Anwar retained the support of Sabah's Gabungan Rakyat Sabah and Sarawak's Gabungan Parti Sarawak, he could continue serving his term until February 2028, even if more MPs aligned with Rafizi Ramli decided to resign.
"I believe Anwar remains focused on governing the country, and the political shifts currently underway have both pros and cons.
"Political negotiations regarding new alignments are taking place. In the future, PMX (Anwar) may be able to restore PH's strength in preparation for the 16th General Election," he said.

Title: North Korea fires ballistic missile towards East Sea: Seoul
Article:
SEOUL: North Korea fired at least one ballistic missile, Seoul's military said Saturday, a day after Pyongyang called the South "despicable" for demanding an apology over a blast in the demilitarised zone that wounded three of its soldiers.
"Our military detected a ballistic missile launched from the Wonsan area of North Korea toward the East Sea," Seoul's Joint Chiefs of Staff said, referring to the body of water also known as the Sea of Japan.
Pyongyang has denied being behind the landmine blast last month inside the Demilitarised Zone (DMZ), the heavily mined buffer dividing the two Koreas since their 1953 armistice.
Seoul as well as the US-led United Nations Command said the blast was caused by North Korean mines laid on the South Korean side of the border.
South Korea's military earlier this week demanded an official apology from the North.
A day later, South Korea's dovish President Lee Jae Myung urged Pyongyang to return to dialogue.
Kim Yo Jong, the powerful sister of North Korea's leader, called Seoul "despicable" Friday, once again denying Pyongyang was behind the blasts.
--AFP

Title: Melaka election: Pas' willingness to use BN logo signals pragmatic approach
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Pas' willingness to contest the Melaka election under the Barisan Nasional logo shows that the latter now has stronger bargaining power, especially in the state.
This is particularly so as it seeks to consolidate Malay votes and avoid clashes between similarly-minded parties.
However, this is not simply a case of Pas "bowing" to BN, say analysts.
Rather, Universiti Malaya political analyst Dr Tawfik Yaakub said the move suggests both sides are willing to put electoral considerations ahead of party symbolism as they negotiate how to maximise their strengths in Melaka.
"I see it as Pas being more pragmatic in seeking a formula that allows the party to remain relevant and competitive.
"I do not see this move as a desperate move but rather as a step to avoid vote splitting and open up room for cooperation with a party that has a strong machinery and influence in Melaka," he told the New Straits Times.
Tawfik said the Registrar of Societies' suspension of Perikatan Nasional's activities had also prompted Pas to explore other options.
He said Pas still had the option of using its own logo, but the final decision would depend on seat negotiations, the form of cooperation and which option would benefit the party most in the election.
On the response from Pas' supporters, Tawfik said it could vary from one area to another and depend on how the decision was explained.
"Some supporters may accept it as a tactical move to avoid clashes and increase the chances of victory.
"However, we should not dismiss the possibility that some may feel uncomfortable, as the Pas logo carries its own sense of identity and loyalty (wala')," he said.
[[nid:1546583]]
Tawfik said the risk of grassroots rejection could be reduced if negotiations resulted in a fair seat allocation, locally accepted candidates and a clear explanation that using the BN logo was intended to facilitate electoral cooperation.
He said the Melaka election could serve as an early test of the cooperation, particularly if it produced clear benefits and strengthened future negotiations.
"If not, I think both parties may return to pursuing their own respective strategies," he said.
Tawfik's UM colleague, sociopolitical analyst Professor Datuk Dr Awang Azman Awang Pawi, said the willingness to use the BN logo should be viewed as political flexibility rather than Pas surrendering its autonomy.
"It can be seen as a sign that both parties are increasingly willing to prioritise electoral strategic compatibility over the importance of symbols alone.
"If Pas genuinely agrees to use the BN logo, it would also imply that BN is becoming a point of unity in the cooperation," he said.
Awang Azman said the response from Pas' grassroots could be one of the biggest challenges for the party leadership.
He said some Pas supporters had a strong attachment to the Pas logo of a white moon on a field of green, which had been the party's identity for decades.
"Any change in logo would naturally require an explanation to the grassroots.
"However, acceptance could be easier if the leadership could explain that using a shared logo is merely an electoral instrument and does not mean Pas is abandoning its identity or organisational principles," he said.
He said the Melaka election could serve as a testing ground for the level of trust between BN and Pas.
"If both sides can resolve the issues that are usually the most difficult in any political cooperation such as seat allocations, candidates and symbols, it would indicate that their relationship has entered a more practical stage," he said.

Title: Budget 2027: Can Malaysia make its tax framework more M&A-friendly?
Article:
Businesses pursue M&A for a myriad of commercial reasons including pursuing rapid inorganic growth, expanding market reach, unlocking synergies, or raising funds.
While "doing a deal" still ultimately involves either selling shares or assets, its art has become more complex over the years through innovative mechanisms like earn-outs, locked box accounts, and M&A insurance.
Anchored by strong GDP growth of 6% in 2026 Q2, Malaysia is expected to continue to have a robust M&A scene building on the strong momentum from previous years. Healthcare and education sectors continue to attract domestic and foreign interest due to its cost competitiveness relative to Singapore and Hong Kong, while benefiting from world-classcinfrastructure and access to the broader Asean market through Malaysia's strategic location.
Deal momentum is also picking up in the local data centre space, attracting those seeking to earn stable yields from the early movers that have shifted from greenfield to the operating space. There is also sector consolidation across industries such as financial services and insurance as well as grocery and consumer retail optimising efficiencies in response to regional supply chain shifts and digital infrastructure demands.
Building a robust M&A tax framework is therefore necessary against this backdrop. Ideally, it should balance between stimulating transactions and adapting to increasingly complex cross border deals, while ensuring the correct amount of tax is collected.
Since the introduction of Capital Gains Tax (CGT) on unlisted local shares in 2024, the tax authorities have made a concerted effort to provide guidance to taxpayers navigating the new regime. For example, their confirmation that tax treaties which provide CGT relief would generally be respected on a self-assessment basis was well received.
Yet certainty is only one part of an effective M&A tax framework. The other is ensuring that tax outcomes keep pace with commercial reality. Currently, CGT must be paid within 60 days of signing the deal, with an additional 30 days being allowed under certain circumstances. A deferral to a much later date is allowed only if the transaction is conditional upon prior approval from the federal or state government—a concept relevant for real property transactions, but perhaps less so for shares.
While parties may have signed the dotted line, it is common deal practice that various key conditions must be satisfied first before the deal is legally completed. These "conditions precedent" could include securing consent from creditors and extending tenancies, typically subject to a deadline. Except for customary "earnest deposit," the seller typically receives the full price only upon completion as there is a risk that the deal may still crumble if all conditions cannot be met. Satisfying conditions therefore could take longer than 90 days depending on complexity.
In simpler words, the current CGT regime effectively taxes the seller on a share sale which has not happened yet—and could still be uncertain pending fulfilment of conditions. The timing of paying CGT could be further enhanced, not only to align with deal reality, but also to create awin-win situation for taxpayer and taxman as it avoids having to deal with CGT refunds if the transaction is rescinded.
Entrepreneurial SMEs, especially those with diversified interests, often reorganise their businesses prior to an M&A transaction. This is typically undertaken to facilitate investors in a common holding company or where the M&A target is a particular business segment only. While it is commendable that tax exemptions are provided for internal restructuring, there may be scope to make them more effective in practice. For example, some of them still require taxes to be paid first followed by a refund later, while others require prior approval from the tax authority.
A friendlier approach could be to allow these exemptions to be enjoyed first without paying taxes, accompanied by monitoring through tax audits in line with the self-assessment spirit. This would help conserve cash flows as these internal exercises are not profit-driven. Liberalising them would also enable speed in execution, which is critical in an M&A. Providing for tax neutrality on qualifying corporate reorganisations would also be much welcomed.
While these could be quick fixes, bolder moves are required to move Malaysia up the ASEAN M&A chain, particularly amidst intense regional competition for capital. Singapore has an M&A scheme which offers tax benefits such as M&A allowance, stamp duty relief, and double deduction on transaction costs to encourage local companies, especially SMEs, to grow through strategic acquisitions. Malaysia could consider something similar especially as SMEs form the backbone our economy—contributing roughly 39.7 per cent of the GDP in 2025.
While tax will always be an important deal consideration, it is often not, and should not be, a deal breaker as the wider M&A thesis must take precedence. Tax is ultimately part of the overall deal economics and parties will seek to manage it appropriately within the confines of the law.
Stability and predictability of the tax landscape is crucial to fully unlocking our country's M&A attractiveness.
Gan Pei Tze is the Partner and Head of Deals Tax, PwC Malaysia. Lee Boon Siew is the Director of Deals Tax, PwC Malaysia

Title: Gold's US$4,100 slide may not mean cheaper gold for Malaysians [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: The sharp correction in international gold prices may not translate into equally steep savings for Malaysian consumers, as the ringgit, type of gold product and seller spreads also determine local retail prices.
Spot gold fell as much as four per cent on Monday to around US$4,111 an ounce, its lowest level since August 5, amid rising US Treasury yields and expectations of further Federal Reserve (Fed) rate hikes.
It traded around US$4,100 on Tuesday before recovering modestly later in the week.
Abdul Razak Gold House (M) Sdn Bhd managing director Mohd Razalie Abdul Rasul said the current decline reflected factors such as interest rates and oil prices.
He reminded Malaysians that international gold prices did not directly determine retail prices.
Mohd Razalie said consumers should look beyond weekly price movements when deciding whether to buy or hold gold.
"A lower international price does not automatically mean a lower price at the counter. The ringgit, the product and the seller's spread all change what a Malaysian actually pays or receives.
"A falling price should prompt questions, not reactions," he said.
Razalie said the correction should also be viewed in the context of gold's longer-term role as a store of value.
"What we are seeing today is a market reacting to interest rates and oil, not a market that has stopped being used as a store of value.
"Those are two different things, and it is important not to confuse them," he said.
SPI Asset Management managing partner Stephen Innes said the main pressure on gold this week had been the rise in US real yields, reinforced by a more hawkish Federal Reserve backdrop.
Whether the correction becomes more sustained, Innes noted that this would depend largely on the Federal Reserve and real yields.
"If real yields keep climbing and the Fed stays hawkish, gold could remain under pressure.
"If yields stabilise, some of that pressure should begin to ease," he told the Business Times.
Upside Capped By Hawkish Fed Bets
Bank Muamalat Malaysia Bhd chief economist Dr Mohd Afzanizam Abdul Rashid said the near-term upside for gold prices appeared somewhat limited as market sentiment remained tilted towards a higher interest-rate environment.
"The fear now is whether the Fed would become more hawkish following the stubbornly high inflation rate with the latest PCE inflation rate sustained at 3.4 per cent during August.
"This could mean the Fed would be inclined to raise rates further to curtail inflationary pressures," he said.
Afzanizam added that the correction could nevertheless provide an entry point for those seeking exposure to gold, particularly given the price's ability to establish a new support level.
"I suppose this could be a good entry point for those who wish to invest in gold.
"What we noticed, despite gold prices having fallen from the all-time high of 5,500 per ounce in the first quarter of 2026, the prevailing gold prices have established a new support base of US$4,000 per ounce.
"This is commendable and the correction from the all-time high level can be deemed healthy as the market adjusts to its so-called new equilibrium price," he said.
Afzanizam added that demand for gold was likely to remain healthy, leaving room for prices to rebound, although investors' holding power, entry points and investment horizon remained important considerations.
For Malaysian investors, Innes said movements in the ringgit would determine how much of the international price decline was reflected domestically.
"A weaker ringgit can cushion some of the decline in US-dollar gold, while a stronger ringgit will make the fall more noticeable locally," he said.
Innes cautioned investors against attempting to pick the exact bottom while real yields remained elevated.
"The recent drop does make gold cheaper than it was a week ago, but investors should still be careful about trying to pick the exact bottom while real yields remain elevated.
"For anyone looking to add exposure, a gradual approach probably makes more sense than going in all at once," he added.
Rate Pressure, Ringgit Cushions Fall
Tradeview Capital fund manager Neoh Jia Man said gold's recent weakness is largely driven by expectations of further interest rate hikes.
As gold does not generate income, higher interest rates increase the opportunity cost of holding the precious metal compared with yield-bearing assets such as US Treasuries, he added.
Neoh said Treasury yields are now at multi-year highs.
With energy prices remaining elevated amid the ongoing conflict involving Iran, markets are pricing in further US Federal Reserve rate hikes in the coming months.
This has resulted in gold falling alongside bonds, rather than performing its traditional role as a hedge.
"Nevertheless, we believe gold remains one of the few effective long-term hedging assets.
"While prices could remain volatile in the near term, investors should continue to maintain a small allocation to gold as part of a diversified portfolio.
Neoh said a stronger US dollar raises the ringgit value of gold, partly cushioning Malaysian investors from declines in global gold prices.
Against this backdrop, he viewed the recent pullback in gold prices as creating reasonable entry points for both consumers and long-term gold investors.

Title: China overtakes US as more positive influence in Latin America: Poll
Article:
BOGOTÁ: China's influence in Latin America is now viewed more positively than that of the United States, a major poll conducted in 17 Latin American countries showed Friday.
The 2026 Latinobarometro survey showed that China overtaking the United States in terms of influence for the first time since the annual survey began in 1995.
It showed 57 per cent of people in Latin America considering the United States to be a positive influence, down from 60 per cent in 2020.
China, meanwhile, was considered a positive influence by 65 per cent of respondents, a jump from 48 per cent six years ago.
Costa Rica and the Dominican Republic were the only countries in the region where US influence was deemed more positive than that of China.
The report partly attributed the shift to Washington's "almost complete absence" from the region in the two decades after the 2003 Iraq War.
During that time, Latin America "drew closer to other powers, to China, to the European Union, to Japan," Marta Lagos, director of Latinobarometer, told AFP.
Lagos said China had won over Latin American populations by allowing them to access cheaper imports.
"The void that China fills is the void in people's pockets, more than anything else," she said.
The growing disaffection towards the United States comes nearly halfway through Trump's second term, during which he has openly asserted his desire for hegemony over Latin America, as part of what he calls the "Donroe Doctrine."
– US POPULARITY DROPS –
As a country, the United States remains more popular than China, with 63 per cent saying they had a favourable view of the world's top economy, compared to 58 per cent for its arch-rival.
But America's popularity was markedly down compared to 2024, when Democratic president Joe Biden was in the White House and 73 per cent had a favorable view of the United States.
The "Donroe Doctrine" blends Trump's first name with that of James Monroe, the fifth US president, who more than two centuries ago declared Latin America the United States' exclusive sphere of influence.
Trump's push to restore US dominance in what Washington calls "our hemisphere" was in evidence in January when the United States overthrew Venezuelan president Nicolas Maduro.
The Latinobarometro poll showed a majority of people in all but one country – Argentina – approving of Maduro's capture by US special forces.
But only 35 per cent considered it benefited Venezuela, compared to 28 per cent who said it harmed the Caribbean country.
Citizens of Venezuela itself were, however, among those who viewed US influence most positively.
Chile-based Latinobarometro is a non-profit organisation that surveys opinions on a range of issues, from democracy to the economy, security and migration.
The 2026 survey was based on some 19,200 face-to-face interviews carried out in 17 countries between May 7 and June 17, with a margin of error of 1 per cent.--AFP

Title: G7 agrees to release 100 million barrels to ease global energy crunch
Article:
PARIS: G7 countries agreed Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil to ease global energy supply concerns, as President Donald Trump hailed the decision and said the US would not impose a threatened diesel export ban.
The announcement came following a video conference of G7 leaders chaired by French President Emmanuel Macron after Washington stepped up pressure on Europe to release strategic reserves and threatened a diesel export ban.
The talks, convened by Macron after a conversation with Trump, focused on coordinating a response to soaring fuel prices among the other G7 economies of Britain, Canada, Germany, Italy, Japan and the United States.
The US-Israeli war with Iran has sent energy prices skyrocketing, coming back to bite Trump at home with high fuel costs that have become a key issue ahead of midterm congressional elections in a month.
Trump had floated the possibility of banning US exports of diesel, which is used in trucks and other hauling vehicles, an alarming prospect for the EU, which relies heavily on fossil fuel imports.
The seven countries agreed to a coordinated release through the International Energy Agency (IEA) of 100 million barrels "to begin immediately over four months, including a frontloaded substantial diesel release within the first 20 days," the leaders said in a statement released by Macron's office.
They also said there would be no ban on diesel exports between them.
"We reaffirm our commitment to refrain from export restrictions on energy and energy products between G7 countries and call on all producers to refrain from imposing bans that could exacerbate market tensions," the leaders said.
"Our citizens' concerns about energy prices remain a top priority."
Trump said European countries had agreed to release a "massive amount" of diesel from their reserves.
"The process will begin immediately," he posted on his Truth Social network.
"Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution – and so are we," Trump said later, adding "Europe did a great thing."
"And we're not going to be doing the export ban," he said.
- US PRESSURE -
Earlier the EU pushed back hard against US threats to impose a diesel export ban, something Macron also warned against during his conversation with Trump.
The flurry of diplomatic activity came a day after US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent cranked up the pressure on European nations.
"American farmers, truckers, and businesses should not be left carrying the burden of a global diesel shortage," he said.
US Energy Secretary Chris Wright likewise held talks with his British counterpart Miatta Fahnbulleh on the crisis, including on the UK's strategic reserves.
British dairy farmer Keith Blackshaw, in the Derbyshire hamlet of Newhaven, complained of a "vicious circle" with high fuel prices being passed onto customers.
"I'd like to see Mr Trump support us a little bit more really," the 69-year-old said. "He looks after his own. Maybe we should do the same, look after our own."
The 32 members of the IEA agreed last March to unlock 400 million barrels of oil from reserves, their largest release ever.
- 'SANCTIONS AGAINST RUSSIA' -
Earlier this week, IEA chief Fatih Birol said European nations had yet to release part of those stocks, which could happen soon.
About a third was yet to come to market, Birol said, adding that further releases were possible since 80 per cent of overall IEA stocks were "still in our pocket."
Diesel prices in the United States and Europe have hit record highs in recent weeks, with an export ban imposed by major producer Russia in response to Ukrainian attacks on fuel facilities also contributing to global market pressures.
The G7 leaders said on Friday: "We will maintain sanctions against Russia while working with the IEA and global partners to prevent further spillovers into fuel, gas, and other commodity markets."
Energy prices surged in the eurozone in September, pushing inflation to 3.8 per cent, the highest level in three years.--AFP

Title: NST COURT WATCH: Taman Sri Muda floods, Zayn Rayyan appeal headline week in court [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: From families seeking compensation after losing their homes in the devastating Taman Sri Muda floods to a dog owner fighting to keep his 15-year-old pet, the courts this week heard cases that put the law against the realities of everyday life.
One of the most significant rulings came from the Shah Alam High Court, which found the government liable for damages suffered by residents during the catastrophic 2021 floods in Taman Sri Muda in Shah Alam.
The court found the Shah Alam City Council (MBSA) negligent, ruling that the local authority remained responsible for maintaining drains and related infrastructure within its jurisdiction.
Also in Shah Alam, Ismanira Abdul Manaf failed in her bid to overturn her conviction and five-year jail sentence for neglecting her six-year-old son Zayn Rayyan Abdul Matin in a manner that caused him physical injury.
In Penang, a dog owner lost his appeal over the seizure of his 15-year-old pet by the Penang Island City Council (MBPP), while in Kuala Lumpur, the High Court upheld an arbitration award requiring Global Wall (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd to pay more than RM77 million to the main contractor of the Merdeka 118 project.
Meanwhile, Sabah's long-running 40 per cent revenue claim also returned to the spotlight after the courts announced that up to 250 members of the public would be allowed to follow an upcoming Court of Appeal hearing through live audiovisual transmission.
Below are some of the major court cases and developments this week.
Government liable over Taman Sri Muda floods
The Shah Alam High Court found the government liable for damages suffered by residents during the devastating floods which hit Taman Sri Muda in December 2021.
The court also held that MBSA was negligent.
Although the council argued that major flood-control assets, including retention ponds and pumping facilities, belonged to the Drainage and Irrigation Department, the court ruled that this did not remove MBSA's own responsibility to maintain drains and related infrastructure within its jurisdiction.
The ruling arose from legal action brought over losses suffered during the floods, which inundated thousands of homes and caused widespread damage in the area.
Zayn Rayyan's mother loses appeal against conviction
The Shah Alam High Court dismissed Ismanira Abdul Manaf's appeal against her conviction and five-year jail sentence for neglecting her six-year-old son, Zayn Rayyan Abdul Matin.
Ismanira had been convicted of neglecting the autistic boy in a manner likely to cause him physical injury.
Zayn Rayyan was reported missing before his body was found near his home in Damansara Damai in December 2023.
The case has remained under intense public scrutiny since his death.
High court upholds RM77 million Merdeka 118 arbitration award
The Kuala Lumpur High Court upheld an arbitration award requiring Global Wall (Malaysia) Sdn Bhd to pay more than RM77 million to the main contractor of the Merdeka 118 project.
The court dismissed 70 challenges mounted by Global Wall against the tribunal's decision.
The dispute arose from works linked to the landmark Merdeka 118 development.
The ruling effectively left the award in favour of the main contractor intact.
Dog owner loses appeal over seizure of pet
The Penang High Court dismissed an appeal by a dog owner over the seizure of his 15-year-old pet during an operation by MBPP.
The court held that the council was entitled to seize the dog after it was found unaccompanied.
The case arose after the animal subsequently died following the seizure.
The proceedings centred on the powers of the local authority to seize unattended dogs and the obligations of pet owners under local council regulations.
Public to get live access to Sabah 40 per cent revenue appeal
Up to 250 members of the public will be allowed to follow the Court of Appeal hearing in Kota Kinabalu on Oct 29 involving Sabah's claim to its 40 per cent revenue entitlement.
The proceedings will be made available through live audiovisual transmission.
The appeal concerns Sabah's constitutional entitlement to 40 per cent of federal revenue derived from the state.
The arrangement is aimed at widening public access to proceedings in a case which has generated considerable interest in Sabah.
Ex-UiTM Holdings CEO charged with CBT involving RM37 million
Former UiTM Holdings Bhd (UHSB) group chief executive officer Azlizan Fadzil was charged at the Sessions Court with criminal breach of trust (CBT) involving RM37.37 million.
The money was allegedly meant for a large-scale solar power project in Gambang, Pahang.
He was accused of dishonestly misappropriating the funds by making payments for purposes other than the intended investment.
Azlizan, 53, who came to court in a wheelchair, pleaded not guilty and was released on bail of RM50,000 with two sureties.
The court also ordered him to surrender his passport, report to the Malaysian Anti-Corruption Commission once every three months and refrain from harassing prosecution witnesses, before fixing Nov 3 for mention.

Title: NST CRIME WATCH: Bullying, rape, shooting and 'dirty dancing' [WATCH]
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: A Form Two student
who died after allegedly being bullied
at a school hostel in Kuala Pilah was beaten with a rubber hose by two senior students before he was found unconscious.
The 14-year-old victim, Muhammad Idlan Fareeq Shahril, was struck repeatedly on the soles of his feet and body with a rubber hose after he was allegedly caught vaping.
Negri Sembilan police chief Datuk Alzafny Ahmad said the two Form Four students were believed to have assaulted the victim after ordering him to retrieve the hose from a bathroom before taking him to two hostel rooms.
Alzafny said they have recorded statements from 69 witnesses, while a post-mortem examination has yet to determine the cause of death.
Following investigations, five other students came forward and told police that they too were bullied by one of the suspects in custody.
Below are some of the crimes reported this week.
Teenager allegedly forced to vape before rape
In Petaling, an 18-year-old woman claimed she was
forced by a man to vape until she lost consciousness
before being raped.
Brickfields police chief Assistant Commissioner Hoo Chang Hook said the incident took place at a residence about 5am last Saturday.
The victim said she regained consciousness two hours later and found herself naked. She also noticed pain in her genital area, leading her to believe she had been raped.
Police are tracking down the suspect.
Man shot at petrol station
In Bidor, Perak, a 41-year-old man was injured after
being shot in the shoulder
by two armed men at a petrol station.
Perak police chief Datuk Mohd Alwi Zainal Abidin said the victim was at the petrol station in a Toyota Land Cruiser when a black Honda City stopped in front of his vehicle.
Two men believed to be armed then got out and fired several shots at the vehicle before fleeing. Five other people inside the Land Cruiser escaped unhurt.
Police recovered a 9mm Luger bullet, four shell casings and bullet fragments at the scene, while CCTV footage from several locations is being reviewed.
Dirty dancing in the city
In Kuala Lumpur, four
foreign male dancers
were detained following an Immigration Department raid on an entertainment outlet in Jalan Klang Lama.
Immigration director-general Datuk Zakaria Shaaban said the premises catered exclusively to male customers, who were charged RM780 per table and entertained by local and foreign male dancers.
He said investigations did not rule out the possibility that arrangements for "extra services" were made between dancers and customers outside the premises.
The four men — three Chinese nationals and a Filipino aged between 21 and 31 — were detained for 14 days under Section 6(1)(c) of the Immigration Act 1959/63.
Three local men were also issued notices to assist investigations, with the findings to be shared with police's Criminal Investigation Department D7 division.

Title: Female US inmate on ventilator after botched lethal injection execution
Article:
WASHINGTON: Convicted US murderer Christa Pike is unconscious on a ventilator after a botched attempt to execute her by lethal injection, her lawyers said in a court filing Friday.
After a dramatic day of legal wrangling, prison officials in Tennessee on Wednesday injected two deadly doses of the highly toxic drug pentobarbital into Pike for the 1995 murder of Colleen Slemmer.
But witnesses said that the 50-year-old Pike remained awake longer than expected and was later heard "loudly snoring" before an ambulance rushed her to a nearby hospital.
Slemmer's mother, May Martinez, who also was in attendance, angrily told a local news outlet that the "state owes me a big apology," and that it had failed her family.
As of Thursday evening, "Ms. Pike remains critically ill and is being treated at a Nashville-area hospital," lawyer Luke Ihnen wrote.
"She is intubated, on a ventilator, and remains unconscious," he added.
The lawyer said medics were "working to save Ms. Pike's life" after she arrived with both arms "swollen, burned, and blistered."
Martinez, who now lives in Florida and raised money to afford the trip to witness the execution, told WJXX television: "All I wanted was justice."
- EXECUTION MORATORIUM -
Pike's was the second failed execution in Tennessee this year.
"After having endured solitary confinement for more than 20 years and a full attempt to kill her by lethal injection, Christa has endured punishment greater than any other person in the history of the American death penalty. The governor must commute Christa's sentence now," another lawyer for Pike, Randy Spivey, said earlier this week.
The state's Republican governor, Bill Lee, who previously denied Pike clemency, halted further executions through the rest of the year while a review is conducted.
Pike's lawyers had argued she should be granted clemency due to her young age and mental health issues at the time of Slemmer's killing. They also cited her history of childhood sexual assault and post-traumatic stress disorder.
"This event is the worst we've seen and unlike any other botched execution in the modern era," Robin Maher, the executive director of the Death Penalty Information Center, told The New York Times. "There is no precedent."
US President Donald Trump questioned how an execution like Pike's could fail, telling reporters that it "shouldn't be very difficult," while UN rights chief Volker Turk urged Tennessee not to make a new attempt to execute Pike.
Had the drugs killed Pike, she would have been the first woman executed by the state in more than two centuries.
In the United States, only 18 women have been executed since 1976, according to the Death Penalty Information Center.--AFP

Title: US voices 'severe disappointment' over G20 trade talks deadlock
Article:
WASHINGTON: The US G20 presidency is "severely disappointed" that some members rejected a statement this week for action against excess industrial capacity, a criticism commonly aimed at China, according to a statement made public Friday.
The United States holds the rotating presidency of the Group of 20 major economies this year, a grouping that also includes China, India, France, Germany and Japan.
But trade ministers failed to reach agreements on countering overcapacity and forced labour after two days of talks in Milwaukee.
A draft ministerial statement against excess capacity, seen as driving costs down unfairly, "was supported by all but a handful of members," said top US trade official Jamieson Greer.
This had called on all countries to move to eliminate structural excess capacity in their economies, among other actions.
Greer's chair statement, made public Friday, did not specify which countries disagreed.
But China in September objected to wording in a finance ministers' statement calling for members to "eliminate non-market policies."
Asked about the topic on the sidelines of G20 talks, China's international trade representative Li Chenggang would only say that parties expressed their respective opinions.
G20 members similarly did not reach a common position on eliminating forced labor from supply chains. Only Mexico and Argentina joined the United States to issue a statement.
Earlier this year, Washington cited concerns over forced labour to slap sweeping tariffs on dozens of economies, including G20 members.
But G20 trade ministers "agreed that trade in food and agricultural products should not be used as a tool for economic or political coercion," Greer's statement said.--AFP
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Trump rules out US diesel export ban after Europe releases fuel reserves
Article:
WASHINGTON: President Donald Trump said Friday that the United States would not impose a diesel export ban, as he hailed a decision by European countries to release the fuel from their reserves.
"Well, it was never really on the table. But what Europe did was a great thing," Trump said at the White House when asked by an AFP reporter if a US export ban was now off the table.
Trump added: "I asked for it. Europe has a lot of diesel and they're going to be making a major world contribution – and so are we.
"And we're not going to be doing the export ban, we're going to be doing what we're supposed to do."
Trump had first said he backed a diesel export ban – which would have cut prices for US consumers but put pressure on supplies elsewhere around the world – on Sept 22.
He said as recently as Thursday that the United States was still considering the idea as his administration put pressure on Europe to tap its supplies.
G7 countries agreed Friday to release 100 million barrels of diesel and crude oil from their reserves over four months to ease global energy supply concerns fueled by the Iran war.
Trump's Republican Party faces losing control of Congress in midterm elections next month amid voter anger over the conflict and its effect on energy prices.--AFP

Title: Lethal injection, nitrogen, firing squads: How US states carry out executions
Article:
THE unprecedented botched execution of a woman in Tennessee has reignited the debate over execution methods in the United States – which varies from lethal injection to firing squads.
The condemned female murderer survived two lethal injections during a botched execution by the US state of Tennessee on Thursday.
Christa Pike, 50, was whisked from a prison execution chamber to a hospital Wednesday night, still alive despite two deadly doses of pentobarbital.
Methods used in the US
Methods vary by state. States carry out the vast majority of executions, while federal executions are rare.
Lethal injection, authorised in 28 states and at the federal level, remains by far the most common execution method since the death penalty was reinstated in the United States in 1976.
Of the 47 executions carried out in 2025, 39 were by lethal injection.
Five others were by nitrogen inhalation, a method first used anywhere in the world in the southern state of Alabama in 2024 and likened by UN experts to a form of "torture."
Three were by firing squad in South Carolina, marking the first use of that method in the United States since 2010.
But some states have struggled to obtain the necessary drugs from pharmaceutical companies reluctant to be associated with capital punishment.
This was the case, for example, in South Carolina, Utah and Indiana, which resumed executions in 2024 after suspending them for more than a decade for this reason.
In terms of frequency, electrocution and gas inhalation are, respectively, most common, each authorised in nine states, followed by firing squads, a method provided for in five states.
A litany of botched executions
No execution method is immune to the risk of spectacular failure.
In Alabama in 1983, John Evans's leg caught fire after the first electric shock, while smoke rose from his hood and the smell of burning flesh began to fill the room.
It took three shocks in all before the condemned man's heart stopped beating.
In the northern state of Ohio in 2009, Romell Broom endured two hours of attempts by three members of the state's execution team, who stuck needles into his arms, hands and legs 18 times in an effort to administer the lethal injection.
The first condemned prisoner to survive an execution attempt in the United States since 1946, he ultimately died of Covid-19 in his cell in December 2020.
Even firing squads, supposedly a more decisive method, present difficulties, Laura Porter, director of a coalition of US organisations campaigning to abolish the death penalty, told AFP.
During Mikal Mahdi's execution in South Carolina in 2025, the shooters, "missed the target of the heart, and so it took longer for [him] to die," she said, citing the autopsy findings.
Nitrogen inhalation was used "with severe, severe problems in Alabama," and "it's temporarily on hold," she said.
"I don't believe that there is a perfect way to kill people," Porter said.
"Participating in execution is incredibly stressful and harmful to corrections officers," she added.
Botched execution consequences
US states generally respond to the most shocking failures by imposing a moratorium to revise their execution protocols or by introducing new execution methods.
Tennessee imposed a moratorium in 2022 before resuming executions by lethal injection in 2025 under a revised protocol.
Alabama tried nitrogen inhalation in January 2024 following a botched lethal injection execution in November 2022.
But Porter said no lasting solution would be possible until the secrecy surrounding executions was lifted.
"When there are problems with protocols, or when there are problems with the drugs, or there are problems with the competency of the execution team, it is very, very difficult to obtain any information until after the problem has happened because we are given no information about the execution process," she said.
* The writer is from AFP

Title: Girl, 8, awarded RM12.19m in medical negligence suit
Article:
MELAKA: The Ayer Keroh High Court today awarded RM12.19 million in damages to an 8-year-old girl in a medical negligence suit involving a government hospital and its doctors.
The girl, who suffered brain damage during birth and was subsequently diagnosed with Spastic Quadriplegic Cerebral Palsy, filed the suit through her father, Mohd Sukri Mahat, 46, who is her legal litigation representative.
Judicial Commissioner Datuk Isa Aziz Ibrahim awarded RM10.77 million in future general damages to cover the plaintiff's lifelong treatment, rehabilitation and multidisciplinary care.
The court, however, rejected a RM220,000 claim for stem cell treatment after ruling that its effectiveness had yet to be established and that it remained experimental.
The girl was also awarded RM500,000 in general damages, RM441,754.83 in special damages, RM300,000 in aggravated damages, RM157,792.22 in pre-trial damages and RM176,718.75 in legal costs and expenses.
Interest of five per cent was also imposed on the relevant damages and judgment sum.
In his judgment, Isa advised the family to manage the compensation carefully for the girl's welfare.
"Although the amount may seem large, it is for 55 years. If calculated, the compensation is only about RM20,000 a month, which I believe is adequate and not excessive.
"What has happened has happened. This is our qada and qadar as Muslims. I hope the amount will not be wasted and will be used as it should," he said.
The suit was filed on Oct 30, 2023, naming 11 defendants, including the Malaysian government, a hospital director and nine doctors. The girl's mother, Noraisah Ali, 42, was initially named as the second plaintiff.
However, the suit against the 10 other defendants was withdrawn and Noraisah's name was removed after the Malaysian government, the 11th defendant, admitted liability on the final day of the trial on June 16.
The assessment of damages took six days from Sept 29 last year, with the plaintiff calling four witnesses, including two experts. The defence did not call any witnesses.
According to the statement of claim, the girl was born on Feb 18, 2018, with APGAR scores of 1, 3 and 4 at 1, 5 and 10 minutes respectively. She required intubation at the fourth minute after being unable to breathe on her own before being admitted to the Neonatal Intensive Care Unit.
An electroencephalogram conducted on the same day showed moderate to severe neonatal encephalopathy.
An MRI scan on March 9, 2018, showed severe injuries to several key brain structures. Subsequent examinations between 2019 and 2023 confirmed the diagnosis of Spastic Quadriplegic Cerebral Palsy, which affects movement in all four limbs.
The girl was represented by lawyers Nur Maizatul Syakira Hashim and Mohamed Fadly Zakariya, while Senior Federal Counsel Norafiah Saini represented the Malaysian government.

Title: Four named suspects in deadly Java Sea ferry sinking
Article:
JAKARTA: Indonesian police have named four suspects in connection with the Virgo Transport 8 ferry that capsized and sank in the Java Sea on Sept 13.
South Kalimantan police Sigit Haryono said the suspects were the ship's captain, an official from shipping and logistics company PT Virgo Karya Shipping, the company's branch manager and its operations manager.
He said the captain was being held at the South Kalimantan police headquarters, while the other three suspects had been summoned for questioning.
As of today, 80 victims had been found dead, while 108 survived and 55 remained missing, according to the National Search and Rescue Agency.
The ferry, carrying 243 people, departed Surabaya in East Java on Sept 12 for Banjarmasin in South Kalimantan.
It encountered bad weather during the voyage and lost contact at around 2am local time on Sept 13.

Title: Nepal's nightmare and the case for climate accountability
Article:
IT  is peak climbing season in the Himalayas. But a Nepali friend, a mountaineering guide, laments how the devastating Aug 26 glacial flood   at  the Nepal-Tibet border is having a dampening effect on the tourist trade impoverished Nepal heavily relies on.
This friend works only a few months in a year, during spring and autumn when mountain trekkers come, to support a wife and young child through the entire year.
As trekker numbers are down  to a trickle, he considers changing jobs but there are few which pay a decent, liveable wage.
That is also the reason why many Nepalis are driven to find better-paying jobs abroad, including Malaysia.
Life may be tough on the roof of the world, but climate change is making it infinitely worse.
How can it be good publicity when images of the ferocious and sudden flood wiping out whole mountain-side settlements, leaving nearly 1,500 dead and thousands more missing and presumed dead (including  Malaysians) were carried globally on TV screens, newspapers and social media.
There is then the rebuilding, which includes repairing more than a dozen hydropower dams and rehabilitating lives in the affected regions —  the estimates of which are reportedly in the billions of US dollars.
Foreign aid, like foreign travellers, is trickling in ever so slowly and proving woefully inadequate to the tasks confronting an inexperienced new government in Kathmandu, which came to power following much political upheaval.
Nepal's plight brings into sharp focus not just the ill effects of climate change writ large,  but also the corresponding issue of climate justice.
Like most poor or developing countries, Nepal contributes precious little of the greenhouse gases that are causing climate change, historically or presently.
Despite this, Nepal and other developing nations are on the front line in feeling the most devastating effects of what climate change can bring.
If global warming continues apace  or  worse, accelerates, the collapse  of ancient glaciers high up in the Himalayas may become an even more common occurrence.
One shudders to think how much worse the ensuing devastation may become. Equally, one must question if anything adequate can be found by way of mitigating future calamities.
Is the relocation of entire populations the only true  solution, whether we are talking about those living high up in the Himalayas or islanders on small Pacific Ocean atolls facing rising sea levels from global warming?
Nepali Prime Minister Balendra Shah's address to the United Nations General Assembly on Sept 24 drew attention to the "Himalayan Tsunami" just a month earlier.
Apart from the loss of thousands of lives (confirmed dead or missing), he said the destruction  was equal to about a tenth of Nepal's gross domestic product.
Shah also proposed a joint regional framework involving Nepal, India and China to share satellite data, monitor glacial lakes and upgrade early warning systems.
Most critically, he called on wealthy countries (and major polluters) to provide grant-based financing instead of loans for managing climate disasters.
Will the world take heed?
* The writer views developments in the nation, region and the wider world from his vantage point in Kuching
© New Straits Times Press (M) Bhd

Title: Trump holds sway over who wins Nobel Peace Prizes
Article:
UNITED States President Donald Trump will not win this year's Nobel Peace Prize as he wages war with Iran, but his influence will still be felt by the awarding body that picks the laureate, according to experts.
Last year's award, to Venezu-ela's Maria Corina Machado, was unique in the prize's 125-year history, coming amid repeated lobbying by Trump to get the award.
Weeks later, Machado gave her gold Nobel medal to Trump, in a bid to win support for her efforts for a democratic Venezuela.
This year, the five-strong body will be mindful of picking someone who can withstand pressure from Trump, according to Haakon Gjerloew, acting director of the Peace Research Institute Oslo.
"I think last year's events around the Nobel Peace Prize, Maria Corina Machado giving it to Trump afterwards, will affect some of the considerations that they make," he said.
"One worry the committee might have is whether awarding it to someone could put them under pressure from  Trump. I think the committee will consider whether the award does more harm than good."
That could mean an award to Pope Leo, the International Criminal Court (ICC), the International Court of Justice (ICJ) or Francesca Albanese, the UN special rapporteur on the Occupied Palestinian Territories, experts say.
The announcement is on Oct 9.
Leo, the first US-born pope, has said he would continue to speak out against war, after the president called him "weak" for criticising the US conflict with Iran.
The pope's encyclical on artificial intelligence, his advocacy for dialogue and the peaceful resolution of conflicts, his calls for respect for migrants and his humanitarian work could justify a prize.
"The pope stands (for) more than just as a religious figure. He has emerged as a leading thought leader," Karim Haggag, director of the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute, said.
Italy's Albanese, meanwhile, has been under fire from the US and Israel for her criticism of Israel's conduct of its war against Hamas in Gaza and the occupation of the West Bank.
To be sure, last year's shock events could have the opposite effect on the committee: go for a safe, uncontroversial choice less likely to antagonise Trump, who blamed Norway —  where the award is decided —  for not giving him the accolade last time.
That could mean recognising Sudan's Emergency Response Rooms, a Sudanese network of community groups providing aid during the civil war, or non-governmental group Save the Children for helping children in conflicts.
But the committee is also under scrutiny to address Trump's challenges to the international order the committee cherishes, said Oeivind Stenersen, a historian who has written about the Nobel Peace Prize.
"They have a certain pressure ... to be tough against Trump," he said.
"In this serious international situation, this year calls for a Peace Prize in defence of liberal democracy, international law and human rights."
This could mean honouring the ICC at a time when Washington is preparing sweeping sanctions against the global tribunal, according to sources, while an award to the ICJ would support respecting the sovereignty of nation-states and resolving disputes peacefully.
Trump has reportedly been nominated by the leaders of Cambodia, Israel and Pakistan, but his chances were "quite low", according to Gjerloew.
Trump's pressure on the Norwegian Nobel Committee has stunned many, including Nobel Peace Prize laureate Maria Ressa, a Filipino and American journalist, who said she watched last year with "horror".
"Bullies don't run the world," she said during a visit to Oslo in September. "There are standards we live by. Might doesn't make it right."

Title: NST Leader: Make Borneo postings feasible for doctors
Article:
IT is that time of the year when newly appointed government medical doctors in the country report for work to their assigned hospitals or clinics. Based on the latest news reports, there is an alarming rate of no-shows by these doctors when they learn they are being posted to Sabah and Sarawak. The Sabah Malaysian Medical Association chairman Dr Brandon Patrick Senagang was even quoted in the
NST
as saying the shortage of medical doctors in the state has reached a "breaking point". Of 138 medical officers from outside Sabah expected to report to their postings, he said, only a shocking 47 officers had done so. Sarawak faces a similarly dire doctor shortage, with even the main hospital in Miri, the state's second city, reportedly afflicted. Health Ministry data showed that the number of medical officers who failed to report for permanent appointments rose from 78 out of 3,215 offers in 2022 to 1,118 out of 5,489 offers in 2023. These are rather concerning statistics.
The reasons for doctors from the peninsula rejecting calls to serve in either Sabah or Sarawak may have much to do with the perceived distance, more so if the postings  are located in more remote locations. This being the case, the Health Ministry must examine if incentives offered for relocating from the peninsula to Borneo adequately reflect the challenges of serving in East Malaysia for doctors from the peninsula. Financial incentives matter, particularly for doctors posted far from their families. The Malaysian Medical Association (MMA) has proposed restoring the percentage-based Borneo Incentive (BIW) payments instead of the fixed rate as currently exists. Additional incentives may include housing assistance, transport support and retention bonuses, with the MMA suggesting that relocation costs be paid in advance rather than later through a laborious claims process.
However, the government needs to go beyond such practical and financial incentives. Perhaps the Borneo postings can be made more attractive by  attaching other incentives,  such as  faster access to specialist training opportunities. In other words, while sweeteners may be offered to help overcome the perception of  hardship postings, the ministry should build a more compelling case that accepting Borneo postings will put such medical officers on a fast track to career advancement. The urgency of filling openings for doctors in the two states cannot be emphasised more strongly enough. A serious lack of doctors in most hospitals there means existing doctors are forced to pick up the slack, further reinforcing the perception of both states as hardship medical postings. The medical profession may be a noble calling but the government does have a vital role in easing the practical constraints doctors may face in accepting calls to serve in Sabah and Sarawak.

Title: Malaysia launches first multi-purpose mission ship in Türkiye
Article:
KUALA LUMPUR: Malaysia's first Multi-Purpose Mission Ship (MPMS 1) for the Malaysian Maritime Enforcement Agency (MMEA) has been launched in Istanbul, Türkiye, marking another milestone in maritime security cooperation between the two countries.
The Home Ministry said the vessel was launched at Desan Shipyard today in a ceremony officiated by Home Minister Datuk Seri Saifuddin Nasution Ismail.
The ceremony was witnessed by Türkiye's Interior Minister Mustafa Çiftçi, Industry and Technology Minister Mehmet Fatih Kacır, Turkish Naval Forces commander Admiral Ercüment Tatlıoğlu and Desan Shipyard representative Cenk İsmail Kaptanoğlu.
In a statement today, the ministry said MPMS 1 was scheduled to be fully completed and begin its voyage to Malaysia by the end of January next year.
The launch included the symbolic breaking of a bottle containing seawater from Malaysia before the vessel was launched into the Sea of Marmara.
"The construction of MPMS 1 is a manifestation of the close relationship between Malaysia and the Republic of Türkiye, particularly in maritime security and enforcement," the ministry said.
It said the acquisition of the strategic asset would strengthen MMEA's operational capabilities in safeguarding the security and sovereignty of Malaysian waters.
The project is also expected to pave the way for greater cooperation between Malaysia and Türkiye in shipbuilding, maritime industry development, and the sharing of expertise and technology.
"The cooperation reflects both countries' commitment to expanding their mutually beneficial strategic relationship," it said.
Saifuddin also held a bilateral meeting with his Turkish counterpart on the sidelines of the launch.
The ministry said the meeting discussed issues of mutual interest, including efforts to strengthen bilateral ties and explore further cooperation and technology-sharing opportunities, particularly in the security and maritime industries.
It said the cooperation could serve as a catalyst for new areas of collaboration while supporting the government's efforts to strengthen the preparedness and capabilities of the country's security assets.
